column2: Thus, tiger among men, I have told you of the excellent Garjiteshvara, which destroys all sins by mere remembrance.
Yudhishthira said: How, dear sinless one, did Daruka practise austerity long ago? I wish to hear the procedure that destroys all sins.
Markandeya said: I shall tell you the wonderful ancient event that took place there among the sages of cultivated self.
The charioteer of the wielder of the thunderbolt was named Matali; long ago he cursed his son for some cause or other.
Trembling because of the curse, the son clasped the lovely feet of Indra and made his plea to the king of the gods, O Bharata:
Cursed by my father and without a protector, lord of the gods — by what deed will this dreadful curse come to an end?
Shakra said: "Resort to the bank of the Narmada and propitiate Maheshvara; stay there until the end of the age, and you will be born again.
Born again in the Yadu family with the name Daruka, you will carry the lord of the gods who bears conch, discus and mace,
when he has taken human form there; then you will attain perfection." Thus addressed by the thousand-eyed god, O Bharata,
he bowed his head to the ground and came away, his lustre gone; resorting to the bank of the Narmada, he wasted his own body
with vows and fasts of many kinds, devoted to japa and oblations; the great-souled Mahadeva, the boon-giving trident-bearer,
he worshipped with supreme devotion until the deluge. Then, at the descent of a portion of Vishnu, he became a man of great wisdom,
and having pleased the lord of the world he went to the good goal. This is the origin of Darutirtha, dear one of good vows,
which I have told you as Shankara told it to me. Then King Yudhishthira, his mind filled with wonder,
looked about bewildered, his hair standing on end again and again. A man who bathes at that holy place according to rule, lord of men,
performs the twilight worship there and satisfies the ancestors and gods, and who gives up his body right there with a collected mind,
obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice and delights in Shiva's presence. Whoever, pure, feeds a brahmin at that holy place with devotion
obtains the excellent fruit of feeding a thousand brahmins. Bathing, giving, austerity, oblation, Vedic study, offerings to the ancestors —
whatever good is done there, one obtains all of it imperishably.
Long ago in the war of gods and asuras, Indra with the hosts of gods was violently driven from his kingdom by danavas proud of their strength.
Their army crushed by masses of elephants, horses, chariots and vehicles, battered by blows, they scattered and took to the road.
Oppressed by the mighty Jambha, Shumbha, Nishumbha and others, together with the Hunda and Grahaka demons, they all approached Brahma.
Bowing their heads to the god Brahma, the supreme lord, the gods headed by Indra and Agni made their plea to the lord of the gods:

Look, look, fortunate one: we have been thrown into confusion by the danavas; oppressed along with our sons and wives, we have come to you alone for refuge.
skandapuran:75:7	Protect us, lord of the gods, Grandsire of all the worlds; we have no other refuge, lord of the gods, but you, the supreme lord.
Brahma said: "To destroy the danavas, resort to the bank of the Narmada and practise austerity, gods, for austerity is the supreme strength.
There is no other means, no mantra, no knowledge and no valour, apart from the holy water of the Reva, which destroys all sins.
Poverty, disease, death, bondage and calamities — these are the fruits of sin; such is my view.
Knowing this, practise hard austerity according to rule; let Shambhu's linga be worshipped by all, and then you will obtain freedom from fear."
Hearing these words of Brahma, the supreme lord, all the gods headed by Indra and Agni then came to the Narmada
and practised there vast austerity, supremely hard to bear; by their resolve, O king, they attained supreme perfection.
From that time the holy place has been known as Devatirtha; it is sung in all the worlds as the destroyer of all sins.
Whoever bathes there with devotion, with a faithful mind and following the rule, obtains the fruit of liberation.
Whoever worships that god, worshipped by all the gods, obtains the excellent fruit of the horse sacrifice.
Whoever feeds brahmins at that holy place, lord of men, likewise; there is the lovely Devashila, which increases great merit.
For men who die there in renunciation the goal is imperishable. Whoever enters the fire at Devatirtha, Yudhishthira,
dwells in Rudra's world until the deluge. Thus bathing, japa, oblation, Vedic study, worship of the gods —
good or evil deeds alike — become imperishable at that holy place. So much is the rule declared, and the origin too, O Bharata,
the account of Devatirtha, unsurpassed among all holy places.
Its full extent in the Purana I cannot now tell, because of my great age, for I have lived a very long time.
Long ago brahmins equal to the gods dwelt in the Daruvana — celibate students, householders, forest-dwellers and ascetics;
for those devoted to their own dharma the supreme state has been declared. Then in the spring season, for some reason or other,
Mahadeva, travelling with Uma in his aerial car, saw the settlement resounding with the sound of the Vedas,
a dwelling of those who come and go, destroying all sins. Seeing it, the god spoke to the delighted goddess in a voice choked with joy,
pointing to the ascetics' wives: "They meditate on no other god and no other dharma, daughter of Himalaya."
Hearing these words spoken by the god of gods, she was seized with curiosity and spoke again to Shankara:
These women whom you called devoted to their duty to their husbands — become the bodiless Love among them and shake their virtue, lord.
Mahadeva said: "What you have said, goddess, does not please me, beloved; the brahmins are highly blessed, and one should not do what displeases them.
Brahmins have wrath as their weapon, Hari has the discus as his weapon; wrath is sharper than the discus, so one should not anger a brahmin.
Neither those gods nor those worlds, neither those nagas nor asuras are seen in the three worlds who, having angered them, were not undone.
One who disturbs them generally falls from the fruit of heavenly enjoyment; those with whom the highly blessed brahmins, gods on earth, are pleased
have dharma, wealth, desire and liberation, no doubt. Knowing this, fortunate one, give up this insistence.
This is contrary to the world's order, if you wish for happiness under control." The Goddess said: "I am not your beloved, god, nor am I under your control.
Bring an unjust affront on all of them here, you of good vows; in Lokaloka nothing is impossible for you, mighty Mahadeva.
Do this for me, god; this is my great curiosity, lord." Thus addressed, Mahadeva, devoted to the goddess's pleasure and good,
took the form of a Kapalika and went to the Daruvana; the moon-crested god bound his mass of matted hair with great serpents,
put on a fine armlet of heron plumes and golden earrings, wore a tiger skin, and was adorned with necklaces and bracelets;
making the earth shake with the jingling of his anklets, with the sound of a great damaru and the ringing of a hero's bell,
he went to the Daruvana when dawn had come. At that time all the brahmins, who lived on flowers, roots and fruits,
had gone out with many others, reciting here and there. Seeing that greatly wondrous form of the god, O Bharata,
the young women became giddy and troubled by desire; seeing that supremely beautiful form, all those fair-faced women,
the women in the Daruvana, fell into distress; many changes came over them on seeing the god who was swift as the mind.
Hear, best of kings, what befell the brahmins' wives: they did not notice their garments slipping, their hands raised;
wishing to give alms, they could not move. One, proud of her beauty and youth, on seeing Mahadeva,
forgot the child sitting on her lap, which fell; another, struck by Love's arrows, pressed her breasts with her arms;
another sighed and could say nothing at all. Thus Mahesha shook all the women whose god was their husband.
Knowing themselves stirred, they hurried out of their doors; the god Maheshvara, having gathered them all together in great excitement,
having shaken the throng of women, then vanished. Then all the brahmins returned and saw
that all the women had been shaken by Hara, and they were filled with anger. One enraged brahmin ran with his staff raised,
another with an axe in his hand, another with a fistful of darbha grass; they all wandered here and there through that forest,
and then, gathering together, the great-souled ones spoke in anger: "If anything has been given or offered in oblation, if our teachers have been pleased,
by that truth let the god's linga fall to the ground." Thus by the power of truth in the words of the twice-born,
the god's linga fell to the ground while he watched. There was a great cry of woe throughout Lokaloka, O Bharata:
the god's linga had fallen, a great ruin for the world. As the linga fell there was a dreadful sound;
mountain peaks fell and the oceans dried up. When the god's linga had fallen, the gods and danavas in their aerial cars
all came together with Brahma, the supreme lord, and with joined palms praised the god with many kinds of hymns.
Then the lord of the world was pleased and became the giver of boons to the gods. The god too, his linga fallen to the ground by the curse,
went to the Daruvana and propitiated the brahmins, O Bharata. Vishvamitra, Vasishtha and the rest, Jabali and Kashyapa,
all came together and said to the destroyer of the Tripuras: "Even the great should not despise the strong; you are lord of the gods;
endowed with forbearance, you will be free from weariness. Since the brahmins' wives were led astray, this excellent linga of yours
that has fallen, Mahadeva, shall become holy. That merit is not obtained by the agnihotra or the agnishtoma;
the bliss, Rudra, that men will obtain by worship of the linga — for gods, yakshas, gandharvas, serpents and rakshasas,
by the word of the brahmins, this shall be holy. Whatever fruit comes from the sight of Brahma, Vishnu, Indra and Rudra,
one shall obtain that whole fruit from the sight of this linga." Thus addressed, the lord of the world bowed to the best of the twice-born,
and filled with supreme joy he replied to them: "Brahmins are a moving holy place, without water, granting all desires,
by the mere utterance of whose words impure people are purified. No holy place, no field, no barren land or cave
is declared better than a brahmin, going to whom one is purified. The holy places on earth, and the rivers headed by the Ganga,
are not worth a sixteenth part of a single word of a brahmin." Having honoured all the twice-born, the great seer took his leave,
and then Mahadeva went to the excellent bank of the Narmada; undertaking a supreme vow, dwelling in a cave for a great ten crores of years,
the Blessed One kept silence, ever devoted to japa and meditation. When the observance was complete, dear one, he installed Maheshvara
and, saluted by the gods, the lord went to Kailasa. Because the supreme Lord was installed on the bank of the Narmada,
for that reason he is the excellent Narmadeshvara. Whatever the best person does, others do likewise;
whatever standard he sets, the world follows. A man who bathes at that holy place according to rule, with senses well controlled,
and worships Mahadeva, gains the fruit of a horse sacrifice. Whoever offers the ancestors sesame, flowers and kusha water,
his twenty-one generations rejoice in heaven, son of Pandu. Whoever, best of men, feeds brahmins according to his means,
by the power of the holy place his gift becomes imperishable. Whoever gives gold or silver to brahmins, Yudhishthira,
touching water as he gives, gains the fruit of the agnishtoma. One should worship especially on the eighth and the fourteenth;
reaching Narmadeshvara, the fruit of birth is attained. Whoever dies there by entering fire or water or by fasting,
his goal is one of no return, as Shankara told me. Whoever recites this account of the excellent Narmadeshvara,
or hears it with devotion, O king, gains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
Whoever gives a tawny cow at that holy place, king of kings, for as many as are the pores on its body and among its offspring,
for so many thousands of years is he honoured in Vishnu's world. The man who dies at that holy place in water, by entering fire, or by fasting
is never again born from a womb. Thus the whole rule has been declared, best of kings;
and the holy fruit of the holy place — what else do you ask? It is blessed, bringing fame and long life, excellent, destroying all sorrow;
hearing this, O king, a man is freed from all sins. Then, king of kings, one should go to the excellent Karanjeshvara,
where a daitya renowned in the world attained perfection, fortunate one. Yudhishthira said: Who was that perfected one of great austerity at that holy place, fortunate one?
Whose son was he, what was his purpose and in what age? Tell me, brahmin. Markandeya said: Long ago in the first age, O king, the mind-born son of Brahma,
knowing the truth of the Vedas and Vedangas, was named Marichi. To him too, O sinless king, after a long time,
a mind-born son was born, Kashyapa, like another Brahma in person. Patience, self-control, compassion, generosity, truth, purity and uprightness —
these qualities of Marichi were present and shone in him, O Bharata. Knowing such a host of virtues and such fame in Kashyapa, best of the twice-born,
Daksha the Prajapati gave him his own daughters as wives: Aditi and Danu and eleven others,
whose sons and grandsons were born as countless brothers. Aditi bore sons headed by Indra;
nagas, pretas and pishachas, birds, yakshas and rakshasas, lions, tigers and boars — the others bore these and the like.
They were born to Kashyapa the Prajapati, mighty-armed one, and by them the three worlds, the great moving and unmoving, were filled.
And another, a fortunate son of Danu, was born, endowed with all auspicious marks, named Karanja.
Like Bali, fortunate one, he practised a very great austerity; the lord, destroyer of the Tripuras, tempted him with a boon:
O Karanja of great strength, I am well pleased with you, sinless one; choose a boon — blessings on you — whatever is in your mind.
Karanja said: "If you are pleased with me, god, lord, destroyer of the Tripuras, then grant me wealth together with sons and grandsons."
Saying "So be it," Mahadeva with Uma, mounted on the bull and with his ganas, vanished right there.
When the god had vanished, the daitya too, filled with joy, installed Mahadeva under his own name and went home.
From then on that holy place has been the excellent Karanjeshvara; by merely bathing there, O king, a man is freed from the killing of a brahmin.
Whoever at that holy place, great king, satisfies the ancestors and gods obtains the holy fruit of the agnishtoma, without doubt.
Whoever fasts to death at that holy place, best of men,
or gives up his life in fire, in water or on the ground, surely dwells in heaven for twenty thousand years.
At the end he is born wealthy in a good and large family, knowing the truth of the Vedas and Vedangas, skilled in all the shastras,
a king or the equal of a king, no doubt, blessed with sons and grandsons and free from all diseases.
All this I have told you, as you asked me: the fruit of the holy place, rightly understood, among all gifts, O Bharata.
This excellent account of the greatness of the holy place is holy, removes sin, is blessed and destroys sorrow for those who recite and hear it.
Whoever causes it to be heard at a shraddha, being devoted to his ancestors, for him everything becomes imperishable; so said Shankara.
Knowing that a son had just been born, Brahma, Grandsire of the world, well pleased and accompanied by sages and gods, gave him a name:

Since you are born of Vishravas and have become my grandson, the name Vaishravana is given to you by me, sinless one.
skandapuran:78:8	You yourself will be the guardian of wealth for all the gods, the fourth of the world-guardians, imperishable, lord of the yakshas.
The yaksha, best lord of the yakshas, had a son, Kundadhara. Reaching fine form and age, with his mother's and father's permission,
he practised vast austerity resorting to the bank of the Narmada, where there is the linga Vyaghreshvara and the excellent Vyaghrakhetaka.
There Kundadhara practised a most terrible austerity: in summer he stood amid five fires, in the rains he endured the downpours,
in winter he stood in water, living on air for a hundred years. When a hundred years were complete he stood on one toe,
turning like a wheel to face the sun, bull among the Bharatas. At the end of the fourth and fifth centuries the bull-borne god was pleased:
Choose a boon, child, whatever pleases your mind; I will give it without doubt, for I am pleased by your austerity.
Kundadhara said: "If you are pleased with me, god, and have come here wishing to grant a boon, then let there be a linga and a holy place here named after me."
Saying "So be it," Mahadeva with Uma vanished; entering the sky he went to Kailasa, upholder of the earth.
When the god had vanished, the yaksha too, filled with joy, installed the lord of the gods, the excellent Kundaleshvara.
He adorned an elephant and a cow with incense, flowers and unguents, and worshipped the linga with canopies, chowries and umbrellas;
he satisfied the brahmins well with food, drink and ornaments, and having propitiated Mahadeva he went to his own home.
From that time, Yudhishthira, that supremely holy place called Kundaleshvara has been famed in the three worlds.
Whoever at that holy place, devoted to fasting, worships the god Ishana is freed from all sins.
Whoever gives gold or silver, gems or pearls to brahmins here rejoices in heaven as a chief among them.
A twice-born man who bathes at that holy place and recites a single verse from the Rik, Yajus or Saman obtains the fruit of the four Vedas.
Hear, son of Pandu, the fruit of one who gives a cow or food to brahmins at that holy place:
for as many as are the hairs on it and among its offspring, for so many thousands of years is he honoured in the world of heaven,
and he dwells in heaven with his sons and grandsons. At that holy place, fortunate one, a thirsty tiger
was wandering in the forest out of fear of the Nishadas; fleeing in fear of the Nishadas, it fell into the water of the Narmada.
Drowned in the water, fortunate one, it took the form of a linga, and a voice from the sky proclaimed it the unsurpassed Vyaghreshvara:
It shall be worshipped in the three worlds and attain renown, without doubt. Whoever bathes at that holy place and worships that linga
is freed from the killing of a brahmin and other sins, no doubt. This I have told you, O king, the excellent Kundaleshvara;
by hearing and reciting it one gains the fruit of a thousand cows.
Yudhishthira said: I wish to hear the story of Pippalada, lord, and the greatness of that holy place where the great ascetic attained perfection.
Whose son was he, fortunate one, and why did he practise austerity? Tell me all this in detail, sinless one.
Markandeya said: Dwelling in Mithila, fortunate one, Yajnavalkya, master of the Vedas and Vedangas, formerly practised vast austerity.
The wise Yajnavalkya's sister, an ascetic, also lived there serving him and practising great austerity.
Then one day, after bathing at the end of her period, she put on an undergarment, having seen a karkataka in private.
That night Yajnavalkya, with that same garment, after a dream released his seed, and at dawn he searched for it again.
Then the brahmin woman said: "What are you looking for, dear one? What do you need, lord? Tell me truly."
Yajnavalkya said: "Good lady, I had an impure dream last night; I had left my white cloth here, and it cannot be seen."
Hearing this, the brahmin woman became greatly frightened, O king: "After bathing, brahmin, I used that cloth as an undergarment."
Hearing her words, the great ascetic cried "Alas!" and suddenly fell to the ground like a tree cut at the root.
As he was saying, "What is this?", a voice came forth from the sky and, consoling the brahmin, spoke then, O king:

I see no fault in him, nor in you, lady of good vows; as for the conception in your womb, fate is supreme in that.
skandapuran:79:14	It must not be destroyed until the time has run its course. Saying "So be it," she, ashamed and dejected from the disgrace,
guarded that embryo until a son was born. As soon as the child was born, telling no one,
she went to an ashvattha tree and left him on the ground: "Whatever beings there are in the worlds, unmoving and moving,
let them protect this child" — and she abandoned him. Having said this, the virtuous brahmin woman, best of kings,
went back as she had come, after lingering a moment. The child threw out his feet and hands, rubbed his lovely eyes,
twisted his face and wept aloud like an orphan; at that sound all beings, unmoving and moving, were terrified,
and he shook the earth with its mountains, forests and caves, dear one. Then, knowing him to be a great being, a bull among the twice-born, overcome by hunger,
the tree did not withdraw its shade and gave him its sap; he was nourished by it as if by nectar, O Bharata. Then, filled with thought, he considered the course of the planets.
Glanced at by him with a fierce look, Shanaishchara, the slow-moving one of cruel conduct, suddenly fell to the ground.
The child even touched Shanaishchara with his foot; afflicted by the child, Shani then said:
What wrong have I done you, brahmin Pippalada, great sage, that as I was moving in the sky I have been thrown down to the ground?
Thus addressed by the son of the Sun, the great sage Pippalada, wrath incarnate, spoke these words; hear them, lord of men:
Why do you, evil-minded one, torment a child bereft of father and mother, son of the Sun? You are spared only by a remnant.
Shanaishchara said: "My gaze is born of a cruel nature, best of the twice-born; release me, and I will do what you say, no doubt."
Pippalada said: "From today, for sixteen years from birth, you must not afflict children; this is your supreme covenant."
Saying to him "So be it," the slow-moving one bowed to the best of sages and went back by the path of the gods as he had come;
then that great planet vanished there. Pondering alone, the child was clouded with anger;
meditating on the south-eastern quarter he produced fire, and cutting his flesh he offered it into the fire according to the true method of generating a kritya.
At once a kritya was born, adorned with garlands of flame, in form like the fire, and she said: "What shall I do?
Shall I dry up the ocean? Shall I grind a mountain to dust? Shall I bring down the vault of the sky and wrap up the earth here?
On whose head shall I fall, and whom shall I slay, brahmin? Quickly tell me my task, lest the time pass."
Hearing her words, the great ascetic Pippalada, the corners of his eyes red with anger, said this:
I conjured you up with a great surge of wrath, lovely one; my father is Yajnavalkya — slay him without delay.
Thus addressed, she swiftly went, as if splitting the vault of the sky, to Mithila, where the great ascetic of great wisdom was practising austerity.
As the mighty Yajnavalkya looked along the path of the quarters, he saw that being arrive, blazing like fire and the sun.
Seeing her suddenly approaching, the great sage was greatly frightened; pursued by the being, the brahmin went to King Janaka:
Know that I have come to you for refuge, best of kings; protect me from the great being, if you can, giver of honour.
The king said: "The being born of brahmin power is irresistible and unassailable; though a ruler, I am not able today; go to another, wise one."
Then the great ascetic went for refuge to another excellent king; told the same by him, he went to Indra for refuge:
King of the gods, salutation to you; protect me from the great being. Hearing his words, Indra then said:
I am not able to protect you, for brahmin power is hard to bear. Then the brahmin, best of knowers of Brahman, went to Brahma's abode,
then to Vishnu's abode; though able, they abandoned him out of fear. Then, supremely distressed and despairing of his life, O king,
pursued by the being, he went to Maheshvara. Endowed with the power of yoga, son of Pandu,
he hid in the space between Mahadeva's nail and flesh, so that the god did not see him. The being, blazing like fire and the sun, came up without seeing him
and said to the Lord, "Release him, release him, O Person, release him!" Thus addressed by that being, O Bharata, Mahadeva
revealed the lord of yogis standing between his nail and flesh. Holding back the kritya, which blazed like the fire of doom, the lord of beings
said: "Do not fear, brahmin, and do not go away, great sage." Then Mahadeva said this to the one standing in subtle form:
What are you to do to him, great being, kritya? Tell me. The kritya said: "I was conjured by Pippalada, blazing with anger, lord of the gods;
I shall fall upon his body — know me to be one who cannot be turned aside, lord." Hearing this from the being's mouth, Mahadeva
bound that mighty slayer of Yajnavalkya, and having given fearlessness to the lord of yogis, the chief of brahmins, Yudhishthira,
the god dismissed him and vanished right there. Pippalada too, having sent off that being, was dejected;
bereft of mother and father, he resorted to the bank of the Narmada, single-minded and without food, for sixteen years,
and propitiated the lord of gods, Shankara with Uma. Hara said: "I am well pleased with you, brahmin of good vows, by this austerity;
choose a boon, and I will give you the auspicious thing your mind desires." Pippalada said: "If the Blessed One is pleased with me, if a boon is to be given to me,
be present here, god Shankara, under my name." Thus addressed, saying "So be it" to the great sage Pippalada,
the god, attended by hosts of bhutas, vanished. When the god had gone, Pippalada bathed there in the great water,
installed Mahadeva and went to the northern mountain. A man who bathes at that holy place with devotion and with mantras, O king,
satisfies the ancestors and gods and worships Maheshvara, obtains the unsurpassed fruit of the horse sacrifice;
dying in the presence of Pippaleshvara he goes to Rudra's city. Or if he feeds brahmins with devotion for the sake of the ancestors,
they are satisfied for twelve thousand years and go to the good goal. Whoever gives up his body at that holy place by renunciation,
his goal is one of no return, as Shankara told me. All this I have told you, as you asked me:
the greatness of Pippalada and the excellent Pippaleshvara. This is holy, removes sin, is blessed and destroys sorrow,
releasing from all sins those who recite and hear it.
The Khetaka named Garjana, where there is the auspicious Devashila — whoever bathes there with devotion and satisfies the ancestors and gods,
his ancestors rejoice in heaven well satisfied for twelve years. Whoever honours brahmins with devotion at that holy place, O king,
even with a small gift, has no end to its merit. Yudhishthira said: Which gifts are praised on earth, chief of brahmins,
by giving which with devotion a man is freed from all sins? Markandeya said: Gold, silver, copper, gems and pearls,
the gift of land and cows release a man, radiant one. Whoever brings about the end of his life at that holy place
dwells in Rudra's world until the deluge. Then one should go to Pushkarini, equal to Kurukshetra, O king;
formerly it was called Pushkarini, and in the Kali age it is known as Kurukshetra. Bathing there, one should worship the god Divakara, the mass of radiance.
A gentle man who recites one verse of the Rik obtains the fruit of the Sama Veda, and likewise of reciting the Yajur Veda and the Rig Veda;
or one may recite the three-syllabled mantra meditating on the sun; reciting the Adityahridaya one is freed from all sins.
Whoever bathes at that holy place and honours brahmins according to rule, his gift becomes a crore times greater, no doubt.
On the full moons of Kartika, Magha and especially Vaishakha, on the new moon, at vyatipata, at a transit, at vaidhriti and on Sunday,
a man who bathes at Kurukshetra becomes a follower of Rudra. Whoever dies at that holy place by fasting, in water, in fire or among the five fires
goes to the supreme goal. A brahmin, kshatriya, vaishya or shudra, best of kings,
doing his prescribed work, goes to the goal of the good. Yudhishthira said: Reciting what is one freed from disease, chief of brahmins, knowing one's caste?
Doing what is a living being freed and does he go to the world without sickness? Markandeya said: Listen attentively, O king, to an ancient history
of how a brahmin was released on reaching Guhyatirtha. Long ago there was an excellent brahmin named Govinda.
His wife, a brahmin woman, was well endowed and devoted to her husband; in her he begot a single handsome son.
The boy used to play in the house with childish games. Once the excellent brahmin went to fetch wood;
bringing a load of wood from the forest, he threw it down at the back of the house. The child, who was playing there, was crushed by the load of wood,
and the boy died there, but the brahmin did not know it; the brahmin woman, out of fear, did not tell him.
Again the brahmin Govinda went to the forest.
The brahmin woman said: "Ravana, Brahma's grandson, whom the three worlds feared, was slain by Ramachandra with his sons, ministers and kin.
So without a son there is no happiness in the mortal world or in heaven. He whose fame is proclaimed, whose speech is for heaven,
who gives sweet food for a brahmin — he too has a dwelling in heaven. There is nothing beyond a son's birth and death for joy and sorrow,
nothing beyond the killing of a brahmin and the horse sacrifice for sin and merit. What shall I say, child? There is no happiness without a son."
Lamenting her many kinds of grief again and again, the brahmin woman hid the child when the brahmin came home.
As she lamented thus, the night passed, Yudhishthira; tormented by grief for her son, as she looked at Govinda asleep on the ground,
her husband afflicted by sorrow, the wife saw Govinda, best of kings, to be made of a mass of worms.
Sunk in sorrow upon sorrow at seeing him thus burdened with sin, as she lay sunk in grief, the night passed.
Again at dawn Govinda went to the forest for darbha grass; thus the brahmin did not know that his son had been killed by the wood.
Five days passed while the brahmin woman kept it hidden. On the fifth day the herdsman, having left the fine buffaloes and cows
in the forest, went home to eat; the excellent brahmin Govinda was asked by the herdsman:
While I eat, master, guard the buffaloes and cows. Then the brahmin hurried to the cows and buffaloes
and went among them; as the brahmin guarded them and ran after them, the cows and buffaloes went to the confluence
and entered the water there at the good confluence with the river Reva. As soon as they had drunk the water he hurriedly drove them back;
without intending it he drank the water and washed his lovely eyes, and afterwards came home at the close of day.
Having eaten, Govinda, full of sorrow, went to bed at night, overcome by sleep, wearied by grief and toil.
Again at midnight his wife looked at him and saw his body covered with worms in places and in places free of them.
Again filled with wonder, his virtuous wife, her mind seized with fear, told him of his evil deed.
The wife said: "On the fifth day past, as you threw down the firewood, the boy standing at the back of the house was killed by you unknowingly.
I did not reveal that dreadful sin you had committed; burning day and night with that hidden sin,
I see no ease in your body nor in my own; my sleep has vanished, lord, and my delight with you.
A verse sung by the great sages is heard in the law book of Manu; remembering it again and again at night, my torment does not cease:
'Adharma perishes by confession and grows by concealment; in this world and the next there is no end to sin.'
Reflecting thus, I stayed awake at night, stricken with fear; I see you as made of a mass of worms — what shall I say?
And again, beloved, your body is flooded with the worms of child-murder; in places they bite you, in places they have vanished all around.
Remembering this again and again and pondering it over and over, I know no reason; I ask you, tell me:
a tank, a river, a holy place or a temple — wherever you went, this is its power and no other's, I think."
Thus addressed, the brahmin, O Bharata, delighting in his wife, told her what had happened before, best of kings:

To turn back the cows and buffaloes I went to the confluence of the Narmada; sunk in water up to my navel, I drank the water as I wished.
skandapuran:80:52	I know of no other holy place but the Narmada, best of rivers. Hearing all this, she at once kept a fast,
and the fair lady went with her husband to the confluence. Having bathed according to rule at the confluence worshipped by the gods,
the brahmin with his wife satisfied the lord of the gods, Shankara with Uma; bathing him with the five nectars,
with sandal, garlands, incense and splendid food offerings, he worshipped there the linga and the auspicious goddess Katyayani.
She kept vigil through the night together with her husband; then at clear dawn, having carefully honoured a brahmin
with a gift of a cow, gold, clothing and food, O Bharata, Govinda honoured the good brahmin according to his means.
A voice from the sky declared: "This holy place is Guhyavati"; the linga Guhyeshvara then rose there from Patala,
and the meeting of the Guhyavati and the Narmada became endowed with virtue. Freed from sin, the brahmin went home with his wife.
This holy place removes sin and destroys the killing of a child. Bathing there, reciting, giving a meal to brahmins,
performing shraddha and offering sesame water, one dwells in Shiva's world until the deluge.
The river came forth from the body of Vishvarupa as he performed his service. Long ago in the Daruvana the god was made linga-less by the brahmins;
resorting then to the bank of the Narmada and practising austerity, O king, the god became Vishvarupa, and the best of rivers came forth.
She went to the water of the Narmada, and the confluence became endowed with virtue. A man who bathes at that holy place is not born again into existence;
whatever rite is performed there becomes wholly imperishable. A sarika bird attained perfection by falling at the confluence of the holy place.
Formerly the best of apsarases, by Shakra's curse, unwillingly enjoyed by Chitrangada, fell into misfortune:
Become a sarika bird, fair one, for twenty years; dying in the water of the Narmada at the good confluence of the Vishvarupa...
She was born a lovely sarika bird of many graceful limbs, O king, remembering her former birth, of divine nature, and dwelt on the bank of the Narmada.
Then, when the time had come, she kindled an auspicious fire, and she of good conduct entered it at the good confluence of the Vishvarupa;
bearing a divine body, O king, she reached Shakra's palace. This stretch is called Sarikatirtha.
Whatever rite is done there — shraddha, sacrifice, worship of Shiva — know it all to be multiplied a crore times, by the sight of Meghanada.
Whoever gives up his life there, helplessly or willingly, has no return to the dreadful ocean of worldly existence.
Hear, Yudhishthira, best of men, the five famous lingas, seeing which a man goes to Shiva:
Meghanada, Goshtheshvara, Vagisha, Kakadeshvara and Lakshmeshvara — whoever worships these five lingas in a single day
goes to Shiva in this very body; having obtained the fruit of a crore of sacrifices, he afterwards attains liberation.
I shall tell you an ancient story, sinless one. Long ago Dharmasena was king, the mighty lord of Ayodhya;
he ruled his kingdom with dharma and performed sacrifices with abundant fees. Listening to the dharma shastras and likewise to the story of the Narmada,
having heard it, the king set out for the northern bank of the Reva; he worshipped Meghanada and bathed in the water of the Narmada,
and as the sun rose the lord of men, mounted on a horse, set out northwards and went to Shiva Goshtheshvara.
Having worshipped him according to rule he then went to Vagishvara; bathing there according to rule, the king worshipped Shiva
with sandal, aloe and camphor, incense and lamps as prescribed; then the best of kings, mounted on his horse, came to Kakadeshvara.
